newsitem.title: USA: More spending cuts seen at Motorola - analysts.
newsitem.headline: More spending cuts seen at Motorola - analysts.

text.p: Technology giant Motorola Inc, having warned third quarter earnings will be significantly lower, is expected to report spending cutbacks on Monday as it faces more stiff competition, analysts said.
"They will most likely have charges -- they are adjusting their spending to reflect market conditions," said Mona Eraiba, an analyst for Gruntal & Co.
Motorola said it will report 1996 third quarter earnings after the market closes Monday, October 7.
According to First Call, the consensus of analysts' earnings estimates is $0.35 a share, versus earnings of $0.81 in 1995. The consensus before Motorola's warning was $0.50.
The company declined to comment on the estimates.

"I think there is definitely going to be some consolidation of their semiconductor and messaging, information and media sectors," said Monish Bahl, an analyst for Parker/Hunter Inc, adding the company has already announced limited layoffs in its semiconductor plants and has postponed construction at one site.

On September 11, Motorola warned that sales and order patterns in July and August indicated earnings for the quarter might be significantly below the second quarter's $0.54 a share. The company said the drop may be 25 percent or more.
The company pointed to a general downturn in the semiconductor sector and stiff competition in the cellular phone handset business, especially internationally.

"The semiconductor business is soft and that is something that at some point will turn around," said Eric Buck, analyst for Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "The pricing of (cellular) handsets is something that will be tougher to turn around."
Analysts said they will look carefully at results for September, when the market, particularly in Europe, traditionally starts to pick up after the summer period.

"It's really critical we see a pickup in September," Eraiba said. "My guess is things did improve in September, but they still have excess capacity (in semiconductors) and challenges in the international cellular market they have to deal with."
In July the company said it cut 145 employees at a Texas semiconductor facility, Motorola's first layoffs in more than a decade.
And at an analysts' meeting in July, the company said it expected to cut capital expenditures for its semiconductor group by as much as 50 percent to about $1.3 to $1.5 billion.
The analysts said they expect to see at least some boost in sectors such as modems. The company has begun to ship its cable modem and announced plans to unveil a 56 kilobit per second modem in 1997.
"There are some parts of the business turning up," said Robert Wilkes, an analyst for Brown Brothers Harriman. "Unfortunately for Motorola, their two biggest areas are under pressure."
